The earliest known use of cacao, the tree whose seeds give chocolate, comes from the upper Amazon in what is now Ecuador, about 5,300 years ago. Chemical traces of cacao were found in pots of the Mayo-Chinchipe culture, which pushed back the story of chocolate by some 1,500 years.

From there the tree travelled north. In Mesoamerica cacao became a drink of the elite among the Olmec, the Maya and later the Aztecs. It was frothy, bitter and often spiced with chili, not sweet. People saw it as a gift of the gods, used it in feasts and offerings, and paid tribute and taxes in cacao beans, which also served as small change in markets.

After the Spanish conquest, chocolate reached Spain, where sugar was added. It became one of the American goods of the Columbian Exchange, and the base of a world industry that runs from West African farms to milk chocolate bars.
